readings.c1s1:
<poem>{{smaller|Thanne shal Deth withdrawe, and Derthe be iustice,
And Dawe the dyker deye for hunger,
But if God of his goodnesse graunt vs a ''trewe''.}}</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), vi. 332.}}}}

{{smaller block|He [Charles the Simple] therefore sente him [the Bishop of Rouen] an Ambassade to . . . Rollo, to require a ''true'' or truse for iii. monthes. {{right|''Fabyan'', Chron. (ed. 1559), I. 227.}}}}

¶
'''true''' (trö), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''trued'', ppr. ''truing''. [< ''true'', ''n.'' Cf. ''trow''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1†.''' To verify.
{{smaller block|Be also intreated to have a continuall and conscientious care not to impeach the Parliament in the hearts one of another by whispering complaints, easilier told then tryed or ''trued''. {{right|''N. Ward'', Simple Cobler, p. 81.}}}}
'''2.''' To make true in position, form, adjustment, or the like: give a right form to; adjust nicely; put a keen, fine, or smooth edge on; make exactly straight, square, plumb, level, or the like: a workmen’s term.
{{smaller block|About six sizes of washed emery progressively finer are employed for grinding the lenses to the true figure, or, as it is called, ''trueing'' the lens. {{right|''Byrne'', Artisan’s Handbook, p. 162.}}}}

'''true-blue''' (trö′blö′), ''a.'' and ''n.'' '''I.''' ''a.'' See ''true blue'', under ''blue''.
<poem>{{smaller|For his Religion . . .
’Twas Presbyterian, ''true-blue''.}}</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''S. Butler'', Hudibras, I. i. 191.}}}}
'''II.''' ''n.'' A person faithful to the principles or characteristics of a body or class.
{{smaller block|Be merry, ''true-blue'', be merry; thou art one of my friends too. {{right|''Randolph'', Hey for Honesty, ii. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|“This gentleman”—here Jermyn made a slight backward movement of the head—“is one of ourselves; he is a ''true blue''.” {{right|''George Eliot'', Felix Holt, xvii.}}}}

[Rare.] '''true-disposing''' (trö′dis-pō″zing), ''a.'' Disposing, arranging, or ordaining justly; just. ''Shak.'', Rich. III., iv. 4. 55. [Rare.] '''true-divining''' (trö′di-vī″ning), ''a.'' ¶
'''trugman†''', ''n.'' Same as ''truchman.''

'''truing-tool''' (trö′ing-töl), ''n.'' An apparatus for cutting the face of a grindstone, etc., to keep it true or accurate; a grindstone-truer. ''E. H. Knight.''

'''truish''' (trö′ish), ''a.'' [< ''true'' + ''-ish''<sup>1</sup>.] Somewhat true. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|They perchance light upon something that seems ''truish'' and newish. {{right|''Bp. Gauden,'' Tears of the Church, p. 198.}}}}

'''truism''' (trö′izm), ''n.'' [< ''true'' + ''-ism.''] An undoubted or self-evident truth.
{{smaller block|Conclusions which in one sense shall be true and in another false, at once seeming Paradoxes and manifest ''truisms.'' {{right|''Berkeley,'' Minute Philosopher, vii.}}}}
='''Syn.''' ''Aphorism, Axiom, Maxim,'' etc. See ''aphorism.''

'''truismatic''' (trö-iz-mat′ik), ''a.'' [< ''truism'' + ''-atic''<sup>2</sup>.] Of or pertaining to truisms; consisting of truisms. [Rare.]

'''truité''' (trwē-tā′), ''a.'' [F., spotted like a trout, < ''truite,'' a trout: see ''trout.''] Having the surface covered with crackle of the most minute and delicate sort: noting porcelain and some of the varieties of the hard pottery of Japan.

'''trull<sup>1</sup>''' (trul), ''v. t.'' [Appar. a var. of ''troll''<sup>1</sup>.] To trundle. [Local.]

'''trull<sup>2</sup>''' (trul), ''n.'' [Early mod. E. also ''trul;'' cf. G. ''trolle,'' a trull; Swiss ''trolle,'' Swabian ''trull,'' a thick, fat woman; cf. also ''trollop''<sup>2</sup>.] '''1.''' A low vagrant strumpet; a drab; a trollop.
{{smaller block|I never saw in all my life such an ugly company of ''truls'' and sluts as their women were. {{right|''Coryat,'' Crudities, I. 104.}}}}
'''2†.''' A girl; a lass; a wench.
{{smaller block|Pray, bear back — this is no place for such youths and their ''trulls'' — let the doors shut again.}}

One truly loved or loving; one whose love is pledged to another; a sweetheart. {{smaller block|“Where gat ye your dinner, my handsome young man?” “I dined wi’ my ''true-love.''” {{right|''Lord Randal'' (Child’s Ballads, II. 249).}}}} '''2.''' A truing-tool. '''true-stitch''' (trö′stich), ''n.'' Through-stitch: applied to embroidery exactly alike on both sides of the foundation. {{smaller block|Sister, i’ faith, you take too much tobacco; It makes you black within, as you are without. What, ''true-stitch'', sister! both your sides alike! Be of a slighter work; for, of my word, You shall be sold as dear, or rather dearer. {{right|''B. Jonson'', Case is Altered, ii. 3.}}}} '''true-table†''' (trö′tā″bl), ''n.'' A table for playing hazard. {{smaller block|There is also a bowling-place, a tavern, and a ''true-table'' [var. ''l'', for ''trufe'', ''truffe'', F. ''truffe'' = Pr. ''trufa'' = Sp. ''trufa'', truffle; prob. < L. ''tubera'', neut. pl. (taken later as fem. sing.) of ''tuber'', an esculent root, a tuber: see ''tuber''. Cf. F. ''tartoufle'', < OIt. ''tartuffola'', ''tartoffalo'' (Milanese ''tartuffol'', Venetian ''tartufola''), truffle (> G. ''tartuffel'', ''kartoffel'', potato), also ''tartuffo'', ''tartufo'', truffle; prob. < L. ''terræ tubera'', ‘earth-tubers’: ''terræ'', gen. of ''terra'', earth; ''tuber'', tuber. Cf. ''trifle''1.] A subterranean edible fungus, especially of the ascomycetous genus ''Tuber''. {{smaller|The common English truffle, ''T. æstivum'', is roundish in shape, and is covered externally with polygonal warts. It is black outside, and brownish veined with white inside, and grows in calcareous soils, usually under birch- or oak-trees. Truffles are much esteemed as an ingredient in highseasoned dishes. As there is no appearance above ground to indicate their presence, dogs and pigs are frequently trained to find them by the scent, and scratch or root them up. Many persons also become expert in selecting {{img float|file=century v08 p0311 c2f1.png|width=203px|align=right|cap={{smaller|Truffle (''Tuber melanosporum''). ''a'', section, showing the interior structure; ''b'', an ascus.}}}} the places where they are likely to grow. The most famous field for the production of truffles is the old province of Périgord in France. The commonest species of the French markets is ''T. melanosporum''. ''T. magnatum'' is the garlic-scented truffle of Italy. Other edible species of ''Tuber'' are ''T. brumale'', ''T. mesentericum'', etc. The celebrated potato-like truffle of Italy, etc., is ''Terfezia leonis''. The false truffle, which is frequently sold in the English and continental markets, is ''Scleroderma vulgare'', allied, as is the so-called red truffle, ''Melanogaster variegatus'', to the puffballs. See ''Tuber'', 2, and compare ''tuckahoe''.}} {{smaller block|A dish of ''trufles'', which is a certaine earth nut, found out by an hogg train’d to it, and for which those animals are sold at a greate price. {{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, Sept. 30, 1644.}}}} '''truffled''' (truf′ld), ''a.''
